questions.question: Complete the diagram to show the amino acid sequence coded by a given DNA base sequence.
questions.answer: Trp - Ser - Ser - Lys - Trp (one amino acid in each box, left to right)
steps: Split the 15 bases into triplets: TGG | AGT | AGC | AAG | TGG.
TGG = tryptophan (Trp); AGT and AGC are both serine (Ser).
AAG = lysine (Lys); the last TGG = tryptophan (Trp).
So the boxes read Trp, Ser, Ser, Lys, Trp.

questions.question: Explain why only five amino acids are coded by the DNA sequence shown.
questions.answer: The code is a triplet code: 3 bases code for 1 amino acid, so 15 bases give 15 / 3 = 5 amino acids.
steps: Each amino acid is coded by a triplet of three bases (a codon).
The sequence has 15 bases, which is 15 / 3 = 5 triplets.
So only five amino acids are coded, and the code is non-overlapping so no base is used twice.
Only three different amino acids appear (Trp, Ser, Lys) because TGG is repeated and the code is degenerate (AGT and AGC both code serine).

questions.question: Explain why some amino acids, such as alanine, have more than one genetic code.
questions.answer: The genetic code is degenerate: 64 codons code for only 20 amino acids, so alanine has several codons (GCU, GCC, GCA, GCG).
steps: There are 64 possible codons but only 20 amino acids.
So some amino acids are coded by more than one triplet codon.
Alanine's codons all start GC and differ only in the third base.
This degeneracy means a third-base change is less likely to change the amino acid.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage of the 64 genetic codes that code for amino acids, to four significant figures.
steps: Percentage = 61 / 64 x 100.
Round to four significant figures: 95.31 %.

questions.question: Explain the role of the other three genetic codes that do not code for amino acids.
questions.answer: They are stop codons (TAA, TAG, TGA) that signal the end of translation and release the polypeptide.
steps: Three of the 64 codons do not code for any amino acid.
These are the stop codons TAA, TAG and TGA.
They are recognised by release factors at the ribosome.
This stops translation and releases the completed polypeptide chain.

questions.question: Choose the row of the table showing the mRNA codon and tRNA anticodon for tryptophan.
questions.answer: B: mRNA codon ACC, tRNA anticodon UGG
steps: The table gives TGG as the DNA triplet for tryptophan, read here as the template triplet.
The mRNA codon is complementary to it: T-A, G-C, G-C gives ACC.
The tRNA anticodon is complementary to the codon: A-U, C-G, C-G gives UGG.
A and D are wrong because tRNA contains uracil, not thymine; C does not pair with its codon.

questions.question: Choose the diagram that shows the R group only of the amino acid AzPhe.
questions.answer: B
steps: The R group is the side chain on the central carbon, not the amino or carboxyl groups.
In AzPhe this is CH2 joined to the benzene ring carrying the N3 group.
A also includes the central carbon (part of the amino acid backbone), so it is wrong.
C has no CH2 link and D is only part of the backbone, so B is correct.

questions.question: Name the covalent bond that joins two amino acids in a condensation reaction.
questions.answer: Peptide bond
steps: Amino acids join during translation by condensation reactions.
The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the next.
A water molecule is removed in the reaction.
The new covalent bond formed is a peptide bond (C-N).

questions.question: Draw two circles on the AzPhe diagram to show the parts lost in a condensation reaction.
questions.answer: Circle the OH of the carboxyl group (-COOH) and one H of the amino group (-NH2).
steps: A condensation reaction releases a molecule of water as the peptide bond forms.
The OH comes from the carboxyl group at the right-hand end of AzPhe.
The H comes from the amino group (NH2) at the left-hand end.
Draw one circle round the -OH of COOH and one round a single H on the NH2 (together they make H2O).

questions.question: Suggest why AzPhe is not inserted into proteins in silkworms that have not been selectively bred.
questions.answer: Non-bred silkworms lack the specific tRNA and synthetase enzyme needed to attach AzPhe, so it cannot reach the ribosome.
steps: AzPhe needs its own tRNA whose anticodon pairs with a codon for AzPhe.
That tRNA must be charged with AzPhe by a specific aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase.
Non-bred silkworms lack this tRNA or enzyme, so AzPhe cannot be attached.
Phenylalanine, with its own tRNA, is inserted instead.

questions.question: Calculate the ratio of phenylalanine to AzPhe in a modified silk section of 1100 amino acids (1% natural phenylalanine, 16% replaced).
questions.answer: 5.25 : 1 (phenylalanine : AzPhe)
steps: Natural phenylalanine = 1% of 1100 = 11 amino acids.
16% of these are replaced: 0.16 x 11 = 1.76 AzPhe.
Phenylalanine left = 11 - 1.76 = 9.24.

questions.question: Suggest how inserting an amino acid with a larger R group could affect the properties of silk fibres.
questions.answer: A bulkier R group changes how the chains fold and interact, altering silk fibre strength, elasticity and stiffness.
steps: A larger R group takes up more space in the polypeptide chain.
This changes folding (secondary and tertiary structure) and the bonds formed.
Chains may pack differently, altering the fibre's strength and elasticity.
So the silk's mechanical properties (e.g. flexibility or stiffness) may change.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term semi-conservative replication.
questions.answer: Each new DNA molecule contains one original (parent) strand and one newly synthesised strand.
steps: The double helix separates into two template strands.
Each old strand acts as a template for a new complementary strand.
Each new DNA molecule therefore keeps one parental strand.
The other strand in each molecule is newly made, so the process is semi-conservative.

questions.question: Name one enzyme involved in semi-conservative replication.
questions.answer: DNA helicase (DNA polymerase, DNA ligase or primase are also acceptable)
steps: Semi-conservative replication requires enzymes to unwind and copy DNA.
DNA helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds.
DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides to the new strand.
Any one correctly named enzyme gains the mark.

questions.question: Explain the importance of semi-conservative replication in producing new cells.
questions.answer: Each new cell gets an accurate, identical copy of the genetic information, so daughter cells are genetically identical.
steps: Before a cell divides, its DNA must be copied.
Semi-conservative replication makes new DNA that is an accurate copy of the original.
Each daughter cell therefore receives the same genetic information.
This keeps the genetic information of the new cells the same as the parent.

questions.question: Complete the table showing the percentage of DNA molecules with heavy only, light only or both nitrogen at each stage.
questions.answer: End of stage 1: 100% heavy only, 0 light only, 0 both. End of stage 2: 0, 0, 100% both. End of stage 3: 0, 50% light only, 50% both.
steps: Stage 1: many generations in 15N, so all DNA is heavy only (100%).
Stage 2: one generation in 14N. Replication is semi-conservative, so each molecule has one old heavy strand and one new light strand: 100% both.
Stage 3: another generation in 14N. Each hybrid molecule makes one hybrid and one light-only molecule: 50% both, 50% light only.
Heavy only is 0% from the end of stage 2 onwards.

questions.question: Draw a diagram of two mononucleotides joined in a single DNA strand, using the symbols shown.
questions.answer: Pentose (pentagon) with a base (rectangle) and a phosphate (circle) attached, then the pentose of nucleotide 1 joined to the phosphate of nucleotide 2.
steps: Mononucleotide: draw a pentagon joined by a short line to a rectangle (base) and by another line to a circle (phosphate).
Draw a second mononucleotide in the same way below the first.
Join them with a line from the pentose of the first nucleotide to the phosphate of the second (a phosphodiester bond).
The sugar-phosphate backbone reads circle - pentagon - circle - pentagon, with a base hanging off each pentagon and no line between the two bases.

questions.question: Calculate the distance between one base and the next on one strand, given 10 base pairs per pitch.
steps: One pitch is 3.4 nm and contains 10 base pairs, so 10 bases on each strand.
Distance between neighbouring bases = 3.4 / 10.
Give 2 significant figures to match the 3.4 nm in the data.

questions.question: Explain which of bases P, Q, R or S is adenine.
questions.answer: R is adenine.
steps: Adenine pairs with thymine by two hydrogen bonds, so adenine is Q or R (P and S form three bonds, so they are cytosine and guanine).
A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine. Thymine is a single-ring pyrimidine, so adenine must have a double ring.
Q has a single ring (a pyrimidine, similar to thymine), so it cannot pair with thymine.
R has a double ring and an NH2 group, so R is adenine.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of mRNA with the structure of tRNA.
questions.answer: Both are single-stranded polynucleotides; mRNA is long and linear with codons, tRNA is short and folded with an anticodon and amino acid binding site.
steps: Both are single polynucleotide strands made of nucleotides with ribose and bases.
mRNA is long and linear, carrying codons in sequence.
tRNA is short and folded (clover-leaf shape) with internal base pairing.
tRNA has an anticodon loop and a site at the 3' end for an amino acid; mRNA does not.

questions.question: State the sequence of the first four amino acids coded by the DNA shown.
questions.answer: Methionine - leucine - isoleucine - tyrosine
steps: Read the DNA in triplets: ATG | CTC | ATT | TAC | CAT | CGA.
ATG = methionine; CTC = leucine.
ATT = isoleucine; TAC = tyrosine.
The first four amino acids are Met, Leu, Ile, Tyr.

questions.question: Name the type of each mutation described for the DNA base sequence.
questions.answer: Base 3 becomes C: substitution. Base 6 becomes base 5: deletion. Base 9 becomes base 10: insertion.
steps: Base 3 is replaced by a different base (G to C): a substitution (point mutation).
Base 6 moves into position 5, so the base before it has been lost: a deletion.
Base 9 moves to position 10, so a new base has been added in front of it: an insertion.

questions.question: Explain the possible effects of the three mutations on the amino acid sequence, using the code table.
questions.answer: Substitution: only one amino acid changes (Met to Ile). Deletion and insertion: frameshift, so every amino acid after the mutation can change.
steps: Original: ATG CTC ATT TAC CAT CGA = Met-Leu-Ile-Tyr-His-Arg.
Substitution of base 3 (G to C): ATC CTC ATT ... so the first amino acid becomes isoleucine, the others stay the same. Effect is small (one amino acid), though it could still alter protein shape.
Deletion (base 5 lost): ATG CCA TTT ACC ATC GA = Met-Pro-Phe-Thr-Ile. The reading frame shifts, so all amino acids after the first change.
Insertion (extra base X before base 9): ATG CTC ATX TTA CCA TCG = Met-Leu-Ile (or Met if X is G)-Leu-Pro-Ser. The first two are unchanged but all later ones change.
Insertions and deletions are frameshift mutations and are usually more harmful than a substitution, because the protein is likely to be non-functional.

questions.question: Describe the role of prothrombin in the blood clotting process.
questions.answer: Prothrombin is converted to thrombin, which converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin fibres that trap cells to form a clot.
steps: Prothrombin is a plasma protein that is converted into the enzyme thrombin.
Thrombin is an enzyme that catalyses fibrinogen conversion.
Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin, which forms a mesh of insoluble fibres.
The fibres trap platelets and red blood cells, forming a clot that stops bleeding.

questions.question: Which type of treatment is warfarin? Options: A anticoagulant, B antihypertensive, C platelet inhibitor, D statin.
questions.answer: A - anticoagulant
steps: Warfarin is used to treat blood clots.
It lowers the number of active clotting factors.
Drugs that prevent blood clotting in this way are anticoagulants.
Option A (anticoagulant) is correct.

questions.question: Using the diagrams of warfarin and vitamin K, suggest why warfarin inhibits prothrombin synthesis.
questions.answer: Warfarin has a similar shape to vitamin K, so it binds to the active site of VKOR (competitive inhibition) and less reduced vitamin K is made.
steps: Warfarin and vitamin K both have a similar ring structure with C=O/O groups, so their shapes are similar.
So warfarin fits the active site of VKOR and acts as a competitive inhibitor.
Vitamin K cannot bind, so it is not converted to reduced vitamin K.
Without reduced vitamin K, prothrombin cannot be synthesised.

questions.question: Suggest why people taking warfarin must avoid foods with a high concentration of vitamin K.
questions.answer: High vitamin K competes with warfarin for the VKOR enzyme, so more reduced vitamin K is made and warfarin's effect is reduced.
steps: Warfarin blocks the enzyme VKOR, which makes reduced vitamin K.
Reduced vitamin K is needed to make prothrombin.
Vitamin K and warfarin compete for the same enzyme.
A high vitamin K intake outcompetes warfarin, so prothrombin synthesis partly recovers.

questions.question: Explain how the study shown should be designed so that warfarin and drug X can be compared.
questions.answer: Use similar, equal-sized groups, the same doses and conditions, and measure prothrombin at the same times, repeating the test.
steps: Groups A and B should be large and of the same size, with people of similar age, sex and health, so that differences are due to the drug.
The same dose of each drug and the same amount of vitamin K must be given, by the same method and over the same period.
Prothrombin must be measured in the same way and at the same time(s) in both groups, ideally also before treatment as a baseline.
Repeat or use many people and compare the means, so the comparison is reliable.

questions.question: Explain the nature of the genetic code, using information from the table.
questions.answer: The genetic code is a triplet code, non-overlapping, degenerate and (almost) universal; three stop codons end translation.
steps: Each amino acid is coded by a triplet (three bases) called a codon.
The code is non-overlapping: each base belongs to only one codon.
The code is degenerate: most amino acids have more than one codon.
It is universal across organisms, and TAA, TAG and TGA are stop codons.

questions.question: Give the sequence of amino acids coded for by the bases shown on the antisense strand.
questions.answer: Methionine - alanine - cysteine - proline - isoleucine - leucine
steps: Read the bases in triplets: ATG | GCT | TGC | CCG | ATC | CTA.
ATG = methionine; GCT = alanine; TGC = cysteine.
CCG = proline; ATC = isoleucine; CTA = leucine.
Sequence: Met - Ala - Cys - Pro - Ile - Leu.

questions.question: Explain the possible effects on a protein of a substitution mutation at the 9th base of the strand.
questions.answer: Base 9 is the last base of codon 3 (TGC, cysteine). The mutation could give no change (TGT), a different amino acid (TGG, Trp) or a stop codon (TGA).
steps: Bases 7-9 are TGC, which codes for cysteine.
TGT: still cysteine, a silent mutation because the code is degenerate, so the protein is unchanged.
TGG: tryptophan replaces cysteine (missense). A different R group may alter bonding, tertiary structure and function.
TGA: a stop codon, so translation ends after two amino acids and a short, non-functional protein is made.
The effect therefore depends on which base replaces C.

questions.question: Choose the diagram showing the sequence of events for the hydrolysis of lactose.
questions.answer: B
steps: Lactose (two joined sugars) binds to the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
The bond is hydrolysed and the two separate monosaccharides leave the enzyme.
The enzyme is unchanged at the end.
A shows lactose released still joined; C shows joining (synthesis); D starts with monosaccharides, not lactose.

questions.question: Which monosaccharides are present in lactose? Options: A fructose and sucrose, B galactose and glucose, C glucose and fructose, D sucrose and galactose.
questions.answer: B - galactose and glucose
steps: Lactose is a disaccharide.
Its two monosaccharide units are glucose and galactose.
Fructose is not in lactose (sucrose contains glucose and fructose).
Option B is correct.

questions.question: Which row of the table describes line P and identifies the letter showing the decrease in activation energy due to lactase?
questions.answer: C: line P is the reaction without enzyme; the decrease in activation energy is Q.
steps: Line P has the higher energy peak, so it is the reaction without enzyme.
Activation energy is the energy needed to reach the peak from the starting level.
The enzyme lowers the peak, and the difference between the two peaks is Q.
R is the activation energy that remains with the enzyme, so the answer is C.

questions.question: Explain why substrate concentration affects the rate of reaction of lactase.
questions.answer: At low substrate, more substrate means more collisions with active sites; at high substrate, all active sites are occupied so the rate plateaus.
steps: Enzyme reactions need substrate molecules to collide with active sites.
Increasing substrate increases collisions and enzyme-substrate complexes per second.
Once all active sites are full (saturation), adding more substrate does not raise the rate.
So the rate increases then levels off at Vmax.

questions.question: Calculate the reaction rate (V) at a substrate concentration of 4 a.u. using the given formula.
questions.answer: about 34 a.u. (33.3 if K is taken as 2; accept 33-34)
steps: Vmax is the plateau of the graph: 50 a.u.
K is the substrate concentration at half Vmax (25 a.u.): reading the curve gives about 1.9, so roughly 2 a.u.

questions.question: Draw a circle around one mononucleotide that includes the base labelled R.
questions.answer: Circle the base R, the pentose it is joined to and one phosphate attached to that pentose.
steps: A mononucleotide is one phosphate, one pentose sugar and one base.
R is the base in the right-hand strand, third row.
Draw one loop round R, the pentagon joined to it and the phosphate circle linked to that pentagon.
Do not include the base on the other strand or a second pentose.

questions.question: Which row of the table identifies the bonds labelled S, T and U?
questions.answer: D: S phosphodiester, T covalent, U hydrogen
steps: S is the bond between a phosphate and a pentose in the sugar-phosphate backbone: a phosphodiester bond.
T is the bond joining a base to its pentose: a covalent bond.
U is between the two bases of a pair: a hydrogen bond.
So the row is phosphodiester, covalent, hydrogen (D).

questions.question: Given base P is adenine, which base is labelled Q (A cytosine, B guanine, C thymine, D uracil)?
questions.answer: C: thymine
steps: P and Q are a base pair joined by two hydrogen bonds (two dashes).
Adenine pairs with thymine by two hydrogen bonds.
So Q is thymine (guanine and cytosine form three bonds; uracil is not found in DNA).

questions.question: Complete the diagram to show the DNA density bands after each stage of the Meselson and Stahl experiment.
questions.answer: Stage 2: one band on the middle dotted line. Stage 3: bands at the top and middle lines, each half height. Stage 4: bands at the top and middle lines, top three times taller than the middle one.
steps: Heavy DNA is lowest, hybrid (15N/14N) is in the middle and light DNA is at the top dotted line.
After stage 2: all DNA is hybrid, so one full-height band on the middle line.
After stage 3: 50% hybrid, 50% light, so two bands (top and middle line), each half the height of the stage 1 band.
After stage 4: 25% hybrid and 75% light, so a band at the top line three times the height of the band on the middle line.

questions.question: Which diagram shows the bands at stage 2 if the dispersive theory were correct?
questions.answer: D
steps: In the dispersive theory each new molecule is a mixture of old heavy and new light DNA.
So at stage 2 all the DNA has the same intermediate density.
This gives one band, in the middle position of the gradient.
A and C show two bands (heavy and light, conservative); B also shows two bands, so D is correct.

questions.question: Complete a Venn diagram of components found in DNA only, mRNA only and both, writing two components in each part.
questions.answer: Overlap: phosphate, adenine (also guanine, cytosine). DNA only: deoxyribose, thymine. mRNA only: ribose, uracil.
steps: Both DNA and mRNA are polynucleotides, so both contain phosphate groups.
Both contain adenine, guanine and cytosine, so these go in the overlap.
DNA alone has deoxyribose and thymine.
mRNA alone has ribose and uracil.

questions.question: Complete the passage about warfarin and the clotting process.
questions.answer: Prothrombin is converted to thrombin by prothrombinase (factor Xa); the active site of thrombin binds fibrinogen; a mesh of fibrin fibres and platelets forms.
steps: Prothrombin is converted into thrombin by an activator enzyme (prothrombinase, containing factor Xa).
Thrombin's active site binds fibrinogen.
Thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin fibres.
The fibres trap platelets (and blood cells) to form a clot.

questions.question: Which type of drug is warfarin? Options: A an anticoagulant, B an antihypertensive, C a platelet inhibitor, D a statin.
questions.answer: A - an anticoagulant
steps: Warfarin lowers the number of clotting factors in the blood.
Drugs that stop blood from clotting are anticoagulants.
It is not an antihypertensive, platelet inhibitor or statin.
Option A is correct.

questions.question: Calculate the rate of decrease in clotting time at two days after stopping warfarin, using a tangent.
questions.answer: 4 s per day (rate of decrease of clotting time; accept 3.5-4.5)
steps: Draw a tangent to the curve at day 2, where the clotting time is 21 s.
The tangent passes through about (0 days, 29 s) and (4 days, 13 s).
Gradient = change in time / change in days = (13 - 29) / (4 - 0) = -4 s per day.
So the clotting time is decreasing at about 4 s per day at day 2.

questions.question: Complete the table by filling the empty boxes with monomer names, elements or bond types.
questions.answer: Polysaccharide monomer: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen. Nucleic acid: monomer nucleotide, bond phosphodiester. Protein monomer (amino acid): carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen (sometimes sulfur).
steps: Monosaccharides contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
The monomer of a nucleic acid is a (mono)nucleotide.
Nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester bonds (between the phosphate of one and the sugar of the next).
Amino acids contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, and some also contain sulfur.

questions.question: Describe how an unsaturated triglyceride is synthesised.
questions.answer: Glycerol combines with three fatty acids, at least one containing a C=C double bond, by condensation reactions forming ester bonds and releasing water.
steps: A triglyceride is made from one glycerol and three fatty acids.
Each fatty acid's carboxyl group reacts with an OH group on glycerol.
This is a condensation reaction that forms an ester bond and releases water.
At least one fatty acid has a C=C double bond, so the triglyceride is unsaturated.

questions.question: Which diagram shows a mononucleotide?
questions.answer: B
steps: A mononucleotide is one phosphate, one pentose sugar and one base.

The base is joined to carbon 1 of the sugar and the phosphate to the CH2 (carbon 5) on carbon 4, and carbons 1 and 4 lie either side of the ring oxygen, so the two attachments are on non-adjacent corners of the pentagon.
B shows the phosphate and base on the two sides of the pentagon with one corner between them.
In A, C and D the phosphate and base are joined to neighbouring corners, so they are wrong.

questions.question: Which diagram shows two components joined by a phosphodiester bond?
questions.answer: B
steps: A phosphodiester bond is the covalent bond between a phosphate group and a sugar.
It joins one nucleotide to the next in the sugar-phosphate backbone.
B shows a pentagon (sugar) joined to a circle (phosphate).
A is sugar to base, C is phosphate to phosphate and D is base to phosphate, so none of these is correct.

questions.question: Which diagram shows complementary base pairing?
questions.answer: C
steps: Complementary base pairs are a purine paired with a pyrimidine: here a large rectangle with a small square.
The bases are held together by hydrogen bonds, shown as dashed lines.
C shows a square and a rectangle joined by dashed lines.
A and B use solid lines (covalent bonds) and D joins two rectangles, so they are wrong.

questions.question: For each statement about the new complementary DNA strand and the mRNA strand, tick the correct box.
questions.answer: Guanines the same as template: neither strand. Thymines equal to adenines in template: only the new complementary DNA strand. No adenine present: neither strand.
steps: Template: A T T G G C G A G A A C has 4 A, 2 T, 4 G and 2 C.
New DNA strand: T A A C C G C T C T T G. It has 2 G (not 4), 4 T (equal to the template's 4 A) and contains adenine.
mRNA: U A A C C G C U C U U G. It has 2 G, no thymine (uracil replaces it) and does contain adenine.
So: statement 1 is neither strand, statement 2 is only the new DNA strand, statement 3 is neither strand.

questions.question: Name the process that synthesises an mRNA strand using the DNA template strand.
questions.answer: Transcription
steps: mRNA is made from a DNA template strand in the nucleus.
The enzyme RNA polymerase reads the template and joins complementary ribonucleotides.
This is transcription.
Translation is the later step where the mRNA is read to make protein.

questions.question: Comment on the design of this clinical trial (94 patients, 48 given the drug, 46 controls).
questions.answer: It has a control group for comparison and patients from many countries, but the text gives no randomisation or blinding, which are needed to reduce bias.
steps: A control group is present, so the drug's effect can be compared.
Patients from 18 countries increase how widely the results apply.
The text does not say the groups were randomised or that the trial was blinded.
Randomised, double-blind design would reduce bias and improve reliability.

questions.question: Calculate the volume of drug given each month to a 64 kg patient receiving 2.5 mg per kg, with a concentration of 189 mg per cm3.
steps: Dose = 2.5 mg per kg x 64 kg = 160 mg.
Volume = mass / concentration = 160 mg / 189 mg cm-3.
Rounded: 0.85 cm3.

questions.question: Calculate the number of patients who experienced nausea when 27% of the patients receiving the drug experienced it.
questions.answer: 13 patients (12.96)
steps: The drug was given to 48 patients.
Number with nausea = 27% of 48 = 0.27 x 48 = 12.96.
Patients are whole people, so round to the nearest whole number.
Answer: 13 patients.

questions.question: Complete the diagram showing the base sequence on the other RNA strand.
questions.answer: G  U  C  U  U  U  C (left to right, bottom row)
steps: The two RNA strands are complementary, with A pairing with U and G pairing with C.
Top strand C A G A A A G, so the bottom strand is G U C U U U C.
RNA has uracil, not thymine, so every A on the top strand pairs with U.

questions.question: Describe the bonding in this double-stranded RNA molecule.
questions.answer: Complementary bases pair by hydrogen bonds (A-U, G-C) between strands; phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides within each strand.
steps: Within each strand, nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester bonds.
Between the two strands, complementary bases form hydrogen bonds.
Adenine pairs with uracil by two hydrogen bonds.
Guanine pairs with cytosine by three hydrogen bonds.

questions.question: Explain how the drug, which interferes with mRNA copies of one enzyme's gene, helps patients with AHP.
questions.answer: The drug destroys or blocks the mRNA for one haem-pathway enzyme, so less of that enzyme is made and less toxic porphyrin accumulates.
steps: The drug is a double-stranded RNA that interferes with mRNA.
Its complementary strand binds to the mRNA from the enzyme's gene.
The mRNA is degraded or translation is blocked (RNA interference).
Less of that enzyme is made, so fewer toxic porphyrins build up.

questions.question: Which are the products of lactose digestion? Options: A fructose and galactose, B fructose and glucose, C galactose and glucose, D glucose and glucose.
questions.answer: C - galactose and glucose
steps: Lactose is a disaccharide of glucose and galactose.
Lactase catalyses its hydrolysis by adding water.
This splits lactose into its two monosaccharides.
Option C (galactose and glucose) is correct.

questions.question: Explain how the three-dimensional structure of lactase affects its mechanism of action.
questions.answer: The specific 3D shape of the active site is complementary to lactose, so it binds the substrate to form an enzyme-substrate complex that lowers activation energy.
steps: Lactase's tertiary structure gives it an active site with a specific shape and charge.
Only lactose fits this active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
The bonds in the substrate are strained, lowering the activation energy for hydrolysis.
Changing the shape (denaturation) stops the substrate fitting, so activity is lost.

questions.question: Suggest one advantage of using immobilised lactase.
questions.answer: The enzyme can be reused, so it is cheaper, and the milk is not contaminated by the enzyme.
steps: Immobilised enzymes are held in beads, not mixed into the milk.
They can be recovered and reused.
This lowers the cost of enzyme per batch.
The milk is not contaminated with enzyme.

questions.question: Explain the effects of pH on the activity of free and immobilised lactase, using the table.
questions.answer: Both enzymes work best at pH 5 and lose activity either side of it, but immobilised lactase keeps more activity at extreme pH.
steps: Both enzymes have their highest activity at pH 5 (free 94 a.u., immobilised 98 a.u.) and the activity falls either side of the optimum.
Away from the optimum, extra H+ or OH- ions break ionic and hydrogen bonds, changing the tertiary structure and the shape of the active site, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form.
At pH 2 both are 0 because the enzyme is denatured.

Immobilised lactase is more active than free lactase at pH 3 (38 against 0) and at pH 6 to 8 (e.g. 76 against 63 at pH 6), because the bead protects the enzyme from the surrounding pH so it is less denatured.

questions.question: Suggest how the rate of activity of the lactase could be measured, with units.
questions.answer: Measure the glucose produced per minute (e.g. with a glucose test strip or colorimeter), in mmol dm-3 min-1.
steps: Lactase releases glucose and galactose from lactose.
Measure how much glucose is produced over a fixed time.
Use a glucose test strip or a colorimeter reading.
Express the rate as mmol dm-3 min-1 (or mg min-1).

questions.question: Suggest why most people with congenital lactose intolerance are found in one country.
questions.answer: A founder effect or inbreeding in that population raised the frequency of the recessive allele.
steps: CLI is caused by a rare recessive allele.
If the allele was present in a small founding population, it could become common there.
Inbreeding or a small gene pool raises the chance of two carriers having children.
So the disorder is concentrated in that population.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a nucleotide pair.
questions.answer: Two nucleotides on opposite strands pair through complementary bases joined by hydrogen bonds: A with T (2 bonds) and C with G (3 bonds).
steps: A nucleotide pair is one nucleotide from each of the two antiparallel strands.
The bases pair by complementary base pairing.
A pairs with T by two hydrogen bonds; C pairs with G by three.
Each purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, keeping the helix width constant.

questions.question: Calculate how long it would take, to the nearest hour, to replicate 150 million nucleotides at 50 nucleotides per second from one end.
questions.answer: 833 hours
steps: Time = number of nucleotides / rate.
To the nearest hour: 833 hours.

questions.question: Explain the role of DNA polymerase in a replication bubble.
questions.answer: DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides to the 3' end of each new strand, using the template strand, forming phosphodiester bonds.
steps: DNA polymerase works at the replication fork within the bubble.
It reads each template strand and matches complementary free nucleotides.
It joins each new nucleotide to the growing strand by phosphodiester bonds.
It builds the new strand 5' to 3' on each template.

questions.question: Suggest why each DNA molecule is replicated using many replication bubbles when S phase lasts about 10 hours.
questions.answer: Replicating from one end would take far longer than 10 hours, so many bubbles copy different sections at the same time.
steps: From part (b), replicating 150 million nucleotides from one end takes 833 hours.
A whole human chromosome is about 300 million nucleotides, so one fork is far too slow.
Many replication bubbles (origins) replicate sections in parallel.
This lets the whole DNA molecule be copied within the 10-hour S phase.

questions.question: Explain the role of the four bases in the structure of DNA, using the ring structures shown.
questions.answer: Guanine and adenine are purines (two rings), cytosine and thymine are pyrimidines (one ring); a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, keeping the helix width constant, and the sequence codes for genetic information.
steps: Adenine and guanine are purines with two rings; cytosine and thymine are pyrimidines with one ring.
A pyrimidine always pairs with a purine (A-T, G-C).
This pairing keeps the double helix a uniform width.
The sequence of bases carries the genetic code.

questions.question: Calculate the mean mass of a base pair for E. coli DNA of mass 3.1 x 10^9 Da and 4.7 x 10^6 base pairs.
steps: Mean mass = total mass / number of base pairs.
Standard form to 2 s.f.: 6.6 x 10^2 Da.

questions.question: Calculate the total mass of DNA in grams after three cell divisions (1 Da = 1.67 x 10^-24 g).
steps: Three divisions give 2^3 = 8 cells, each with one copy of the DNA.
Total mass = 8 x 3.1 x 10^9 Da = 2.48 x 10^10 Da.
Mass in grams = 2.48 x 10^10 x 1.67 x 10^-24 g.

questions.question: Complete the diagram showing the results of the Meselson and Stahl experiment.
questions.answer: Stage 2: one full-width band on the middle dotted line. Stage 3: two bands, one on the top line and one on the middle line, each half width.
steps: Heavy (15N) DNA sits on the bottom line, hybrid DNA in the middle and light (14N) DNA on the top line.
After stage 2 all DNA molecules are hybrid (one old heavy strand, one new light strand): a single full-width band on the middle line.
After stage 3 half the molecules are hybrid and half are all light, so there are two bands, each half the width of the stage 1 band.
The light band is on the top dotted line and the hybrid band on the middle dotted line.

questions.question: Complete the diagram showing band positions if the conservative theory were correct.
questions.answer: Stage 2: two bands, a half-width heavy band on the bottom line and a half-width light band on the top line.
steps: In the conservative theory the original double helix stays intact and a completely new molecule is made.
After one generation in 14N there is one all-heavy molecule (the original) and one all-light molecule (new).
The heavy molecule gives a band at the bottom dotted line (as in stage 1) and the light one a band at the top dotted line.
There is no band in the middle line, and each band is half the width of the stage 1 band.

questions.question: Complete the diagram showing band positions if the dispersive theory were correct.
questions.answer: Stage 2: one full-width band on the middle dotted line.
steps: In the dispersive theory each new molecule is a mixture of old heavy and new light segments.
So after stage 2 both molecules have the same intermediate density.
They form a single band at the middle dotted line, with the full width of the stage 1 band.
No bands appear on the top or bottom lines.

questions.question: What type of molecule is pectinase? Options: A disaccharide, B polysaccharide, C protein, D triglyceride.
questions.answer: C - protein
steps: Pectinase is an enzyme.
All enzymes are globular proteins.
Disaccharides, polysaccharides and triglycerides are not enzymes.
Option C is correct.

questions.question: Explain why enzymes are described as biological catalysts.
questions.answer: Enzymes are biological (protein) molecules that lower the activation energy of reactions without being used up.
steps: Enzymes are made by living organisms and are proteins.
They speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy.
They do this by binding substrate at the active site.
They are not used up, so they can catalyse many reactions.

questions.question: Calculate the effect on the rate of reaction of each degree increase between 46 C and 50 C (2 s.f.).
questions.answer: -8.5 a.u. per degree C (the rate falls; accept 8.5 to 8.8)
steps: Read the rate at 46 C from the graph: about 54 a.u.
Read the rate at 50 C: 20 a.u.
Change in rate = 20 - 54 = -34 a.u. over 4 C (50 - 46).
Change per degree = -34 / 4 = -8.5 a.u. per C (2 significant figures), a decrease.

questions.question: State why the rate of reaction decreases above the optimum temperature.
questions.answer: The high temperature denatures the enzyme: bonds in its tertiary structure break and the active site changes shape.
steps: Above the optimum, the enzyme gains too much kinetic energy.
This breaks the hydrogen and ionic bonds holding its tertiary structure.
The active site changes shape (denatures).
The substrate no longer fits, so the rate falls.

questions.question: Draw a diagram of a phospholipid using the information in the table.
questions.answer: Glycerol (hatched rectangle) with one phosphate (circle) and two fatty acids (open rectangles) each joined to it by a bond line.
steps: Draw the hatched glycerol rectangle upright.
Join one phosphate circle to one end of the glycerol with a line (bond).
Join two fatty acid rectangles to the other two positions on the glycerol, each with a line.
The two fatty acids run parallel, side by side, away from the glycerol.

questions.question: Which diagram shows an ester bond?
questions.answer: C
steps: An ester bond is C-O-C=O, formed between a carboxyl group and a hydroxyl group.
It joins a fatty acid to glycerol in a phospholipid.
C shows the carbon, an oxygen link, then a carbon with a double bond to oxygen.
A is a peptide bond (N-C=O), B has no linking oxygen and D has an N-O link, so they are wrong.

questions.question: Explain why an increase in temperature increases the fluidity of the membrane.
questions.answer: Higher temperature gives phospholipids more kinetic energy, so they move more and the bilayer becomes more fluid.
steps: Heating increases the kinetic energy of the phospholipid molecules.
They vibrate and move more vigorously.
Weak hydrophobic interactions between tails are overcome more easily.
The membrane becomes more fluid.

questions.question: Which row of the table describes an unsaturated fatty acid compared with a saturated fatty acid with the same number of carbons?
questions.answer: C: has double bonds between two carbons; fewer hydrogens than the saturated fatty acid
steps: An unsaturated fatty acid has one or more C=C double bonds.
Each double bond means two fewer hydrogens are attached to the carbon chain.
So with the same number of carbons it has fewer hydrogens than the saturated acid.
C is correct.

questions.question: Explain why a decrease in cholesterol increases the fluidity of the membrane.
questions.answer: Cholesterol sits between phospholipid tails and restricts their movement, so less cholesterol means the tails move more freely.
steps: Cholesterol is found between the phospholipid tails.
It packs between the hydrophobic tails and restricts their movement.
Less cholesterol lets the tails move and slide past each other more.
So the membrane is more fluid.

questions.question: Suggest why a fatty acid with a shorter side chain increases the fluidity of a membrane.
questions.answer: Shorter chains have fewer hydrophobic interactions between tails, so they pack less tightly and move more.
steps: Longer chains have more contact (van der Waals) between tails.
Shorter chains have fewer points of contact.
They pack less tightly.
So the membrane is more fluid.

questions.question: Suggest how the fatty acid content of fish membranes may have changed when fish moved to colder water.
questions.answer: The membranes probably became richer in unsaturated fatty acids (and/or shorter chains).
steps: Cold makes membranes less fluid (more rigid).
To counter this, membranes need more fluidity.
Unsaturated fatty acids have kinked tails that pack less tightly.
So the proportion of unsaturated fatty acids increased.

questions.question: Suggest why these changes are necessary for the survival of the fish.
questions.answer: Keeping membranes fluid at low temperature keeps membrane proteins, enzymes and transport working.
steps: At low temperature, membranes would become too rigid.
Rigid membranes stop transport proteins and enzymes working properly.
Keeping the membrane fluid maintains cell function.
So the fish can survive in cold water.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term biological catalyst.
questions.answer: A protein produced by living organisms that speeds up a chemical reaction by lowering its activation energy, without being used up.
steps: Biological means it is made by living organisms (usually a protein).
Catalyst means it speeds up a reaction.
It does this by lowering the activation energy.
It is not used up or changed by the reaction.

questions.question: Which arrow on the energy graph shows the energy required to start the reaction?
questions.answer: B
steps: Activation energy is the energy needed to start the reaction, from the energy of the reactants up to the peak.
Arrow Q goes from the reactant level up to the top of the energy hill.
P is the energy of the reactants above the base line, and R and S are measured from the product level or axis.
So Q is correct.

questions.question: Explain why E1 cannot convert AB into AC or AC into D, using the diagram.
questions.answer: Enzymes are specific: E1's active site fits only A and B, so it cannot bind AB or AC.
steps: Each enzyme has an active site with a specific shape complementary to one substrate.
The substrates of E1 are A and B. AB and AC have different shapes from A and B, so they do not fit E1's active site.
So no enzyme-substrate complex forms, and E1 cannot catalyse AB to AC or AC to D.
Separate enzymes, E2 and E3, are needed for those steps.

questions.question: Describe two conclusions from the table of rates at different pH and temperature combinations.
questions.answer: 1. pectinase works best at pH 4 and 30 C (35 a.u.). 2. At pH 2 or at 60 C there is no activity at all.
steps: The highest rate is 35 a.u. at pH 4 and 30 C, so this is the best of the combinations tested.
At pH 2 the rate is 0 at all temperatures, and at 60 C it is 0 at all pHs, so extreme pH and high temperature denature the enzyme.
At 30 C the rate is much higher at pH 4 (35) than at pH 8 (10), so pH 4 is closer to the optimum.
At 5 C the rate is low (5 a.u.) at both pH 4 and pH 8, so low temperature slows the reaction.

questions.question: Calculate the minimum mass of protein a 70 kg person should eat in one week to reach a synthesis rate of 150 mg per kg.
steps: From the graph a rate of 150 is first reached at a diet of 1.4 g of protein per kg per day (0.9 gives only 130).
Per day for a 70 kg person: 1.4 x 70 = 98 g.
Per week: 98 x 7 = 686 g.
The minimum mass of protein is 686 g.

questions.question: Name the two stages of protein synthesis, in the order they occur.
questions.answer: Stage 1: transcription; Stage 2: translation
steps: Protein synthesis starts in the nucleus with DNA.
Transcription makes an mRNA copy of the gene.
The mRNA then moves to the ribosome.
Translation then builds the polypeptide from the mRNA codons.

questions.question: Describe the roles of mRNA and tRNA in protein synthesis.
questions.answer: mRNA carries the codons copied from the gene to the ribosome; tRNA carries specific amino acids and its anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon.
steps: mRNA is a copy of the gene that carries codons out of the nucleus to the ribosome.
tRNA is a small molecule with an anticodon at one end.
tRNA carries the specific amino acid matching its anticodon.
The anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon, so amino acids join in the correct order.

questions.question: Describe the evidence for and against a relationship between blood cholesterol and heart disease.
questions.answer: For: the curve for people who developed heart disease is shifted to higher cholesterol levels. Against: the curves overlap greatly and have the same maximum.
steps: For: the dashed curve (developed heart disease) peaks at a higher blood cholesterol level, and a bigger percentage of this group have higher cholesterol (to the right of the peak).
For: a bigger percentage of the group who did not develop heart disease have lower cholesterol (left of the peak).
Against: the two curves overlap for most of their length, with similar shapes and the same peak height.
Against: many people with high cholesterol did not develop heart disease, and some with low cholesterol did.

questions.question: Describe the evidence in the HDL and LDL graph that supports the three conclusions.
questions.answer: Incidence of CVD rises with LDL, falls with HDL, and is highest at low HDL with high LDL.
steps: LDL: at every HDL level, the bars get taller as LDL increases (e.g. at HDL below 40, from about 2 a.u. at LDL below 100 to over 6 a.u. at LDL 160 or more).
HDL: at every LDL level, the bars get shorter as HDL increases (e.g. at LDL 160 or more, from the tallest bar at HDL below 40 to a much shorter bar at HDL 60 or more).
Ratio: the highest incidence is at low HDL and high LDL (lowest ratio of HDL to LDL), and the lowest incidence (less than 1 a.u.) is at high HDL and low LDL (highest ratio).

questions.question: Explain how the LDL receptor is involved in endocytosis of LDL.
questions.answer: LDL binds to its specific receptor, which clusters in a coated pit that invaginates to form a vesicle taking LDL into the cell.
steps: The LDL receptor is a membrane protein with a binding site specific to LDL.
LDL binds to the receptor on the outer surface of the liver cell.
The receptor-LDL complex collects in a coated pit that folds in.
The pit pinches off as a vesicle carrying LDL into the cell.

questions.question: Suggest how a change in pH could cause LDL to separate from its receptor.
questions.answer: Lower pH alters ionic and hydrogen bonds in the receptor or LDL, changing their shapes so they no longer bind.
steps: Proteins have ionic and hydrogen bonds that depend on charge.
A lower pH changes the charges on the amino acid R groups.
This alters the tertiary shape of the receptor's binding site.
LDL can no longer bind and is released.

questions.question: Explain why mutations in the LDL receptor gene can increase the risk of CVD.
questions.answer: A mutated receptor may not bind or internalise LDL, so LDL and cholesterol stay high in the blood and build up in arteries.
steps: A mutation can change the receptor's amino acid sequence and shape.
The receptor may fail to bind LDL or be made at all.
LDL is not removed from the blood by endocytosis, so blood LDL and cholesterol rise.
Cholesterol then builds up in artery walls, causing atherosclerosis and CVD.

questions.question: Complete the passage about the structure of DNA.
questions.answer: Phosphodiester bonds form during condensation reactions, releasing water; hydrogen bonds join complementary base pairs; the DNA twists into a double helix.
steps: Mononucleotides are linked by phosphodiester bonds.
These form in condensation reactions, releasing a molecule of water.
Complementary base pairs are held by hydrogen bonds.
The double-stranded molecule twists into a double helix.

questions.question: Draw one DNA mononucleotide using shapes selected from the table.
questions.answer: Pentagon D joined by a line to a circle (phosphate) and by a line to the thymine box T.
steps: A DNA mononucleotide has one phosphate, one deoxyribose and one base.
Use the pentagon marked D (deoxyribose), not R (ribose, found in RNA).
Use the box marked T for the base, not U (uracil, found in RNA).
Draw a bond line from the deoxyribose to the phosphate circle and another bond line from the deoxyribose to the T box.

questions.question: Which arrow shows the activation energy for this reaction?
questions.answer: B: Q
steps: Activation energy is the energy needed to start the reaction.
It is measured from the energy of the reactants up to the top of the peak.
Arrow Q spans this gap; P is the difference between the reactants and the base line (energy released), and R and S are measured from the product level.
So Q is correct.

questions.topic: Molecules At Times Y And Z
questions.question: Which row of the table shows the molecule present at time Y and time Z on this graph?
questions.answer: C: time Y reactant, monophenol; time Z product, o-diphenol
steps: The equation shows that monophenol is converted to o-diphenol.
At the start (time Y) the reactant, monophenol, is present.
At the end (time Z) the product, o-diphenol, is present.
So the row is reactant/monophenol and product/o-diphenol (C).

questions.question: Which row shows how the lengths of arrows P and Q would change when polyphenol oxidase is present?
questions.answer: C: P no change, Q decrease
steps: The enzyme lowers the activation energy, so arrow Q gets shorter.
The enzyme does not change the energy of the reactants or products.
So the energy difference between reactants and products, arrow P, does not change.
So the row is no change for P and decrease for Q (C).

questions.question: Calculate the rate of reaction at 3 minutes by drawing a tangent.
questions.answer: about 9.4 mmol dm^-3 min^-1 (accept 9-10)
steps: At 3 minutes the monophenol concentration is about 25 mmol dm^-3.
Draw a tangent to the curve at 3 minutes; it passes through about (0 min, 53 mmol dm^-3) and (5.6 min, 0).
The rate of reaction at 3 minutes is therefore about 9.4 mmol dm^-3 min^-1.

questions.question: Explain what would happen to the shape of the curve if the temperature increased to the enzyme's optimum.
questions.answer: The curve would become steeper initially and reach its plateau sooner, because more collisions and enzyme-substrate complexes form per second.
steps: Below the optimum, raising temperature increases kinetic energy.
More frequent collisions give more enzyme-substrate complexes.
So the initial rate (slope) increases and the curve is steeper.
The plateau is reached earlier and at a higher rate, as the optimum gives the fastest rate.

questions.question: Complete the diagram showing the base sequence of the mRNA made from the template strand.
questions.answer: U  A  C  G  G  C  A  A (left to right)
steps: mRNA is made complementary to the template strand: A pairs with U, T with A, G with C and C with G.
Template A T G C C G T T gives U A C G G C A A.
RNA has uracil in place of thymine, so there is no T in the mRNA.

questions.question: Name this stage of protein synthesis.
questions.answer: Transcription
steps: The mRNA is made from a DNA template strand.
This happens in the nucleus.
Making mRNA from DNA is called transcription.
Translation is the next stage.

questions.question: Name the enzyme used in this stage of protein synthesis.
questions.answer: RNA polymerase
steps: Transcription needs an enzyme to read the DNA template.
RNA polymerase unwinds DNA and joins complementary ribonucleotides.
It forms phosphodiester bonds 5' to 3'.
So the enzyme is RNA polymerase.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of an mRNA molecule with that of a tRNA molecule.
questions.answer: Both are single-stranded polynucleotides; mRNA is long and linear with codons, tRNA is short, folded and has an anticodon and amino acid site.
steps: Both are single polynucleotide strands with ribose and bases.
mRNA is long and unfolded, with codons in sequence.
tRNA is short and folded (clover-leaf) with some base pairing.
tRNA has an anticodon and an amino acid attachment site.

questions.question: Describe the structure of collagen.
questions.answer: Collagen has three polypeptide chains wound into a triple helix, with repeating glycine-X-Y sequences, stabilised by hydrogen bonds.
steps: Collagen is a fibrous protein made of three polypeptide chains.
The chains are wound together into a triple helix.
Every third amino acid is glycine, allowing tight packing.
Hydrogen bonds between chains give strength.

questions.question: Calculate the rate of reaction at 30 minutes by drawing a tangent.
questions.answer: about 2.5 nmol dm^-3 min^-1 (accept 2.2-2.8)
steps: At 30 minutes the concentration of breakdown product is about 163 nmol dm^-3.
Draw a tangent to the curve at 30 minutes; it passes through about (10 min, 113) and (50 min, 213).
Rate of reaction at 30 minutes = about 2.5 nmol dm^-3 min^-1.

questions.question: Explain how a protease breaks down elastin.
questions.answer: The protease binds elastin at its active site and hydrolyses peptide bonds, splitting the protein into smaller peptides.
steps: Proteases are enzymes that hydrolyse peptide bonds.
The enzyme's active site binds a specific sequence in elastin.
Water is used to break the peptide bonds (hydrolysis).
This splits elastin into smaller peptides and amino acids.

questions.question: Explain how damage to endothelial cells results in the formation of thrombin.
questions.answer: Damaged endothelium exposes underlying collagen and tissue factor, triggering the clotting cascade that converts prothrombin to thrombin.
steps: Healthy endothelial cells prevent clotting.
Damage exposes underlying collagen and tissue factor.
This triggers platelet activation and the clotting cascade.
The cascade converts prothrombin into thrombin.

questions.question: Give one risk of treating patients with anticoagulants.
questions.answer: Excessive bleeding (haemorrhage).
steps: Anticoagulants stop blood from clotting.
This lowers the body's ability to stop bleeding.
So the patient may bleed excessively.
Bleeding (haemorrhage) is the main risk.

questions.question: Which is the minimum number of bases in the gene coding for a 32-amino-acid peptide (A 32, B 33, C 96, D 99)?
steps: Each amino acid is coded by 3 bases: 32 x 3 = 96 bases.
The gene also needs a stop codon (3 bases) to end translation.
Total = 96 + 3 = 99 bases.
Option D is correct.

questions.question: Explain how variegin prevents blood clotting.
questions.answer: Variegin binds to thrombin's active site, blocking it, so thrombin cannot convert fibrinogen into fibrin.
steps: Thrombin needs its active site to act on fibrinogen.
Variegin fits into the active site of thrombin.
It blocks the site (competitive inhibition).
Fibrinogen cannot be converted to fibrin, so no clot forms.

questions.question: Explain how thrombin splits variegin into two molecules.
questions.answer: Thrombin is a protease: its active site binds variegin and hydrolyses a peptide bond, using water, splitting it into two parts.
steps: Thrombin is a protease enzyme.
Its active site binds a specific sequence in variegin.
A peptide bond is broken by hydrolysis, which uses a water molecule.
This splits variegin into two smaller molecules.

questions.topic: Variegin Versus Drug H Clot Mass
questions.question: Comment on the results comparing the effect of variegin and drug H on clot mass in stents.
questions.answer: Clots in stents with variegin are much smaller than with drug H, but there are few results and one overlaps.
steps: Variegin clots are about 11-22 mg, much less than most drug H clots (43-70 mg), so variegin looks more effective at preventing clots in stents.
The mean clot mass for variegin (about 15 mg) is far lower than for drug H (about 47 mg).
One drug H result (about 18 mg) is within the variegin range, and drug H results are very variable.
There are only 4-5 stents per treatment, so more repeats and a statistical test are needed to be confident.

questions.question: Which sugar is present in uridine monophosphate?
questions.answer: D - ribose
steps: UMP is a ribonucleotide, found in RNA.
RNA nucleotides contain the sugar ribose.
DNA nucleotides use deoxyribose instead.
Option D (ribose) is correct.

questions.question: Draw a circle around the base in uridine monophosphate.
questions.answer: Circle the six-membered ring at the top of the molecule (the uracil base), not the sugar or phosphate.
steps: Uridine monophosphate has a phosphate group, a ribose sugar and a base.
The base is the nitrogen-containing ring with two C=O groups and an NH, attached to the sugar through its N.
Draw the circle round this whole ring (with its =O and HN), and stop at the bond to the sugar.
Do not include the five-membered sugar ring or the phosphate group.

questions.question: Suggest one way cells use uridine monophosphate.
questions.answer: To make RNA (it is a nucleotide monomer used in transcription).
steps: UMP is a nucleotide.
Nucleotides are the building blocks of nucleic acids.
UMP can be phosphorylated to UTP.
UTP is used as a monomer to synthesise RNA.

questions.question: State how OMP decarboxylase increases the rate of the reaction.
questions.answer: It lowers the activation energy by binding the substrate at its active site and straining the bonds.
steps: The enzyme binds orotidine monophosphate at its active site.
This forms an enzyme-substrate complex.
The complex strains bonds and orients the substrate.
So less activation energy is needed, speeding the reaction up.

questions.question: Explain why OMP decarboxylase catalyses this reaction only.
questions.answer: Its active site has a specific shape and charge complementary to only its substrate, so only that reaction is catalysed.
steps: The active site's shape and charge are determined by the enzyme's tertiary structure.
Only the correct substrate can bind (lock and key).
Other molecules do not fit, so they are not converted.
Hence the enzyme is specific to this reaction.

questions.question: Describe the roles of RNA in the synthesis of collagen.
questions.answer: mRNA is transcribed from the collagen gene and carries the code to ribosomes; tRNA brings amino acids; rRNA in ribosomes catalyses peptide bond formation.
steps: Transcription makes mRNA copies of the collagen gene in the nucleus.
mRNA carries the code from the nucleus to ribosomes.
tRNA molecules bring specific amino acids to the ribosome, matched by anticodons.
rRNA forms part of the ribosome and catalyses peptide bond formation.
Together these build the collagen polypeptide chains.

questions.question: Explain how the primary structure of collagen determines its properties.
questions.answer: Its amino acid sequence (repeating glycine-X-Y with proline and hydroxyproline) allows the chains to form a tight triple helix, giving strength and insolubility.
steps: The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids.
Glycine at every third position lets the three chains pack closely.
Proline and hydroxyproline stabilise the helix.
The triple helix and hydrogen bonds give collagen its strength and insolubility.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term gene.
questions.answer: A sequence of DNA bases that codes for a polypeptide (or functional RNA).
steps: A gene is a length of DNA.
Its base sequence contains the code for one polypeptide or functional RNA.
Genes are found at loci on chromosomes.
A gene therefore determines a characteristic.

questions.question: Describe how the two strands of DNA in a gene are held together.
questions.answer: By hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs (A-T and G-C).
steps: The two DNA strands are antiparallel and complementary.
Bases on opposite strands pair up.
Adenine pairs with thymine by two hydrogen bonds.
Guanine pairs with cytosine by three hydrogen bonds.

questions.question: Explain why each codon must contain at least three bases.
questions.answer: Four bases make only 16 combinations (not enough for 20 amino acids), whereas three bases give 64 combinations.
steps: There are 20 different amino acids to code for.
A doublet (two bases from four types) gives 4 x 4 = 16 combinations.
16 is fewer than 20, so it is not enough.
A triplet gives 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 combinations, which is enough.

questions.question: Determine the probability that a child of a colour-blind father and a heterozygous mother is colour blind.
steps: Father: X(c)Y (colour blind). Mother: X(N)X(c) (carrier).
Gametes: father X(c) or Y; mother X(N) or X(c).
Offspring: X(N)Y, X(c)Y, X(N)X(c), X(c)X(c), each 1/4.
Colour blind children are X(c)Y and X(c)X(c), so probability = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.

questions.question: Complete the diagram showing how two glucose molecules join by a glycosidic bond to form two products.
questions.answer: Maltose (two glucose rings joined by a C1-O-C4 glycosidic bond) and a water molecule.
steps: Glucose molecules join in a condensation reaction.
The OH on carbon 1 of the first glucose (right-hand carbon) joins with the H of the OH on carbon 4 of the second glucose (left-hand carbon).
Draw the two rings with a single oxygen between C1 of the first and C4 of the second: this is the 1-4 glycosidic bond, making a disaccharide (maltose).
The OH and H removed form the second product, a molecule of water (H2O).

questions.question: Draw one disaccharide and two different oligosaccharides produced by amylase digesting the amylopectin shown.
questions.answer: Disaccharide: the two open circles between the grey circles on the top row. Oligosaccharides: the three open circles at the left end of the top row, and the five-circle chain made of the first grey circle and the four circles below it.
steps: Amylase cuts only 1-4 bonds, so the bonds from a grey circle to the circle below it (1-6 bonds) stay intact.
Cut between the third open circle and the first grey circle, between the first grey circle and the next open circle, and between the last open circle and the second grey circle.

This gives a disaccharide (the two open circles joined to each other), a trisaccharide (three open circles joined) and a pentasaccharide (the first grey circle plus the four circles joined below it, in a line).
Each product has at least two circles, because only disaccharides and oligosaccharides are made (no single glucose).

questions.question: Explain why amylase is able to break only 1-4 glycosidic bonds.
questions.answer: Its active site is shaped to fit the 1-4 linkage of the glucose chain, so it only binds and hydrolyses that bond type.
steps: Enzymes have an active site with a specific shape.
Amylase's active site fits the alpha 1-4 glycosidic linkage.
The 1-6 linkage at branch points has a different shape and does not fit.
So amylase only hydrolyses 1-4 bonds.

questions.question: Suggest how disaccharides and oligosaccharides are broken down in the small intestine, giving reasons.
questions.answer: Specific enzymes on the small intestine lining (e.g. maltase, sucrase, lactase) hydrolyse each disaccharide and oligosaccharide, because each enzyme's active site is specific to one glycosidic bond.
steps: Disaccharides and oligosaccharides are hydrolysed by enzymes on the intestinal wall.
Each disaccharidase (maltase, sucrase, lactase) fits a specific disaccharide.
Oligosaccharides are broken down by enzymes that remove glucose units from the end of the chain.
Specificity of the active site is the reason different enzymes are needed.

questions.question: Explain why glucose cannot diffuse into the bloodstream without membrane transport proteins.
questions.answer: Glucose is a large polar molecule that cannot pass through the hydrophobic phospholipid bilayer of the cell membrane.
steps: Glucose is polar and hydrophilic.
The inner part of the membrane is hydrophobic.
Polar molecules cannot dissolve through the phospholipid bilayer.
A transport protein provides a channel or carrier for glucose.

questions.question: Explain the dipole nature of water.
questions.answer: Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so it pulls shared electrons, giving oxygen a partial negative charge and each hydrogen a partial positive charge.
steps: Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen.
Shared electrons in O-H bonds are pulled towards oxygen.
Oxygen becomes slightly negative and hydrogen slightly positive.
The bent shape means the charges do not cancel, so water is a dipole.

questions.question: Complete the diagram to show a hydrogen bond between two water molecules.
questions.answer: Draw a dashed line from a hydrogen atom (delta +) of one water molecule to the oxygen atom (delta -) of a neighbouring molecule.
steps: A hydrogen bond forms between the slightly positive hydrogen of one water molecule and the slightly negative oxygen of another.
For example, join the upper H of the middle molecule to the O of the right-hand molecule with a dashed line.
Mark delta + on the hydrogen atoms and delta - on the oxygen atoms.
The line must go from an H to an O of a different molecule, not within one molecule.

questions.question: Complete the diagram showing two water molecules around a sodium ion.
questions.answer: Two water molecules touching the Na+ ion with their oxygen atoms pointing towards it and their hydrogens pointing away.
steps: Water is polar: oxygen is slightly negative (delta -) and hydrogen is slightly positive (delta +).
The positive Na+ ion attracts the delta - oxygen atoms.
Draw two water molecules next to the ion with their O atoms nearest to the Na+ and the H atoms pointing outwards.
Label the oxygens delta - (and hydrogens delta +).

questions.question: Describe the effects of temperature on the solubility of chemicals A, B, C and D.
questions.answer: A: solubility rises steadily with temperature. B: rises sharply to about 33 C, then falls slightly. C: almost unchanged. D: falls as temperature rises.
steps: Chemical A: solubility increases steadily (roughly linearly), from about 7 g per 100 g at 0 C to about 85 g at 80 C.
Chemical B: increases rapidly from about 4 g to a peak of about 50 g at about 33 C, then decreases slowly to about 43 g at 80 C.
Chemical C: little effect; solubility stays about 36-38 g per 100 g over the whole range.
Chemical D: solubility decreases as temperature increases, from about 17 g at 0 C to about 1 g at 80 C (the fall is steepest at low temperatures).

questions.question: Name the current model for the structure of the cell membrane.
questions.answer: The fluid mosaic model
steps: The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer.
Proteins are embedded in or on it.
The components move laterally, so it is fluid.
This is the fluid mosaic model.

questions.question: Describe the arrangement of phospholipids in the cell membrane.
questions.answer: Phospholipids form a bilayer with hydrophilic heads facing outwards to water and hydrophobic tails facing inwards, away from water.
steps: Phospholipids have a hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic fatty acid tails.
In water they form a double layer (bilayer).
The heads face outwards to the aqueous environment on each side.
The tails face inwards and are sheltered from water.

questions.question: Calculate the diameter of a lipid nanoparticle with a volume of 0.108 (units as given), using pi = 3.0.
questions.answer: 0.6 um
steps: V = (4/3) x pi x r^3, with pi = 3.0, so V = 4 r^3.
r = cube root of 0.027 = 0.3 um.
Diameter = 2 x r = 0.6 um.

questions.question: Describe the structure of an mRNA molecule.
questions.answer: A single-stranded chain of ribonucleotides (ribose, phosphate and bases A, U, G, C) joined by phosphodiester bonds.
steps: mRNA is a single polynucleotide strand.
Each nucleotide contains ribose, a phosphate and a base (A, U, G or C).
Nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester bonds.
It is linear and carries codons.

questions.question: Explain the arrangement of phospholipids in a lipid nanoparticle that carries mRNA to tissues.
questions.answer: Phospholipids form a sphere with hydrophilic heads facing the watery outside and hydrophobic tails facing inwards, enclosing the mRNA in a protected core.
steps: The nanoparticle is in an aqueous environment, so heads face outwards.
Tails face inwards, away from water, forming a hydrophobic interior.
The hydrophilic, negatively charged mRNA is held in the aqueous core.
This protects mRNA from enzymes and lets it be carried to tissues.

questions.question: Explain why eating soybeans may reduce the risk of heart disease.
questions.answer: Less LDL and cholesterol means less atheroma in the artery walls, so arteries stay wider and clots are less likely, lowering the risk of heart disease.
steps: LDLs carry cholesterol to tissues and deposit it in artery walls, so lower LDL and cholesterol means less cholesterol is deposited.
So less atheroma (plaque) forms, which means less damage to the endothelium and less narrowing of the coronary arteries.
Blood flow to the heart muscle stays high and the risk of blood clots (thrombosis) is lower.
This reduces the risk of coronary heart disease and heart attacks.

questions.question: Give two ways the primary structure of two proteins could differ.
questions.answer: The types of amino acids and the sequence (order) of amino acids can differ, and so can the number of amino acids.
steps: Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids in a chain.
Two proteins can contain different amino acids.
They can also have the same amino acids in a different order.
Either the type, order or number of amino acids gives a valid answer.

questions.question: Explain why the scientists used digested soybeans to make the extract.
questions.answer: Digestion produces the peptides that are absorbed in the gut, so the extract mimics what would reach the liver.
steps: In the human gut, soybean proteins are digested into peptides first.
The peptides, not whole proteins, are what enters the body.
Using digested soybean copies this.
So the results reflect the effect of real absorbed products.

questions.question: Suggest why the soybean flour was incubated with different enzymes in steps 2 and 3.
questions.answer: Different enzymes act at different peptide bonds, copying digestion in the stomach and then the small intestine.
steps: Each protease has a different specificity.
The stomach and small intestine use different enzymes.
Using them in sequence copies the digestive process.
So the soybean protein is fully broken into peptides.

questions.question: Explain why the soybean flour and enzymes were incubated at 37 C for 2 hours.
questions.answer: 37 C is body temperature, the optimum for human digestive enzymes, so they work at their fastest without denaturing.
steps: Human digestive enzymes work best at body temperature.
37 C is the optimum temperature for these enzymes.
This copies conditions in the human gut.
Two hours allows the digestion to proceed to completion.

questions.question: Explain why eating soybeans may reduce blood cholesterol, using the graph of HMGCR activity.
questions.answer: Soybean peptides inhibit HMGCR, so less cholesterol is synthesised by liver cells and blood cholesterol falls.
steps: As the concentration of soybean peptides rises, the inhibition of HMGCR rises from about 5% to nearly 100%.
Over the same range, the synthesis of cholesterol falls from 100% to about 5%.
HMGCR is an enzyme in cholesterol synthesis, so inhibiting it lowers cholesterol production, so less enters the blood.
Therefore eating soybeans (which provide the peptides) may reduce blood cholesterol.

questions.question: Describe the role of RNA polymerase in protein synthesis.
questions.answer: RNA polymerase unwinds the DNA and joins complementary ribonucleotides to form mRNA using the template strand.
steps: RNA polymerase binds to the gene's promoter region.
It unwinds the DNA double helix.
It reads the template strand and joins complementary ribonucleotides.
It forms phosphodiester bonds, producing mRNA 5' to 3'.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of the start and stop codons and how they work.
questions.answer: Both are triplet codons; the start codon AUG codes for methionine and starts translation, while stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) do not code for an amino acid and end it.
steps: Both are triplet (three-base) codons on mRNA.
The start codon AUG codes for methionine and initiates translation.
Stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA do not code for amino acids.
Stop codons are recognised by release factors, which end translation.

questions.question: Describe the roles of ribosomes in protein synthesis.
questions.answer: Ribosomes bind mRNA and tRNA, bringing amino acids together, and rRNA catalyses the formation of peptide bonds.
steps: Ribosomes provide the site for translation.
They hold the mRNA and align tRNAs with their codons.
The ribosome's rRNA catalyses peptide bond formation.
It moves along the mRNA, linking amino acids into a polypeptide.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the genetic code being a triplet code.
questions.answer: Each amino acid is coded for by a sequence of three bases (a codon).
steps: Each codon is made of three consecutive bases.
One codon codes for one amino acid.
For example, GCC codes for alanine.
So the code is read in triplets.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the genetic code being non-overlapping.
questions.answer: Each base belongs to only one codon, so consecutive codons do not share bases.
steps: The code is read in consecutive, separate triplets.
A base in one codon is not used again in the next codon.
This means the reading frame is fixed.
So each base has one specific role in the code.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the genetic code being degenerate.
questions.answer: More than one codon codes for the same amino acid.
steps: There are 64 codons but only 20 amino acids.
So some amino acids have more than one codon.
For example, several codons code for alanine.
Changes in the third base may therefore not change the amino acid.

questions.question: Describe two conclusions from the graph of blood cholesterol and coronary heart disease death rate.
questions.answer: In every region the CHD death rate rises as blood cholesterol rises, and at the same cholesterol level the death rate is higher in Northern Europe and the US than in the Mediterranean and Japan.
steps: For Northern Europe the death rate rises from about 14% at 5.0 mmol dm^-3 to about 29% at 8.3; for the United States from about 10% at 4.9 to about 25% at 7.8, so there is a positive correlation.
Mediterranean and Japan stay low (below about 7%) even at 5.5 or more mmol dm^-3, where the US and Northern Europe have 12-14% or more.
So blood cholesterol is not the only factor, because the death rate differs between regions with the same cholesterol level (other factors such as diet and lifestyle).
Northern Europe has the highest death rate at each cholesterol level.

questions.question: Give two side effects of taking statins.
questions.answer: Muscle pain (myopathy) and liver damage.
steps: Statins lower cholesterol synthesis in the liver.
A known side effect is muscle pain or weakness (myopathy).
Another side effect is raised liver enzymes or liver damage.
Muscle pain and liver damage are the answers.

questions.question: Explain how an increase in LDL receptors helps reduce blood cholesterol levels.
questions.answer: More LDL receptors means more LDL is endocytosed by liver cells, removing cholesterol from the blood.
steps: LDL receptors on liver cells bind LDL particles in the blood.
More receptors means more LDL is bound.
The LDL is taken into liver cells by endocytosis.
So less cholesterol remains in the blood.

questions.question: Calculate the UK population, given about 270 000 people with FH, affecting 1 in 250 people.
steps: Population = number with FH / fraction affected.
In standard form: 6.75 x 10^7.

questions.question: Suggest why statins are less effective in people homozygous for FH.
questions.answer: Homozygous people have little or no functional LDL receptor, and statins work by increasing these receptors.
steps: Statins act by increasing the number of LDL receptors on liver cells.
Homozygous people have two mutant copies of the LDL receptor gene.
They produce little or no functional receptor.
So statins have little effect.

questions.question: Suggest how an antisense strand of DNA from the apo B gene would reduce apo B protein levels.
questions.answer: It binds complementarily to the apo B mRNA, blocking translation or causing the mRNA to be degraded.
steps: The antisense strand is complementary to the apo B mRNA.
It binds to the mRNA by complementary base pairing.
This blocks the ribosome from translating it or marks it for degradation.
Less apo B protein is therefore made.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term semi-conservative replication.
questions.answer: Each new DNA molecule contains one original strand and one newly synthesised strand.
steps: The original double helix separates into two template strands.
Each template is used to make a new complementary strand.
Each new molecule has one old strand and one new strand.
This is semi-conservative.

questions.question: Describe the role of DNA polymerase in DNA replication.
questions.answer: DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides to the 3' end of the new strand, forming phosphodiester bonds, using the template strand.
steps: DNA polymerase reads each template strand.
It matches complementary free nucleotides to the template bases.
It joins each nucleotide to the 3' end of the growing strand.
This forms phosphodiester bonds.

questions.question: Complete the graphs showing the concentrations and densities of DNA at stages 1, 2 and 3 of the flowchart.
questions.answer: Stage 1: one peak at 7.74. Stage 2: one peak at 7.67. Stage 3: two peaks at 7.60 and 7.67, each half the height of the stage 1 peak.
steps: Stage 1: all DNA is heavy (15N) with density 7.74, so one peak at 7.74 of the same height as the reference peak.
Stage 2: all DNA is hybrid (one heavy and one light strand), with density halfway between 7.74 and 7.60, which is 7.67: one peak at 7.67 of the same height.
Stage 3: half the DNA is hybrid (7.67) and half is light only (7.60): two peaks, one at 7.60 and one at 7.67.
Each stage 3 peak is half the height of the stage 1 peak, as each holds half the molecules; there is no peak at 7.74 after stage 1.

questions.question: Explain how two identical molecules of DNA are produced.
questions.answer: The double helix is unwound and each strand acts as a template for a new complementary strand, so two identical molecules form.
steps: DNA helicase unwinds the double helix, breaking hydrogen bonds.
Each separated strand acts as a template.
DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides to each template.
